Vignette: Margaret

Margaret is an eighty-year-old retired social worker who sits with a careful stillness in the therapy room, her hands folded in her lap as though she has spent decades practicing composure. She speaks quietly and precisely, choosing her words the way someone might choose footing on uneven ground. She has lived alone for nearly forty years, and she says this not with sadness but with something that sounds closer to relief.

The abuse began in the early 1970s, when Margaret was in her mid-thirties and working as a newly qualified social worker in a mid-sized English city. She had met Gerald at a colleague's dinner party — charming, educated, the kind of man her mother would have approved of. They moved in together within six months. What followed, over the course of four years, was a sustained campaign of physical violence that escalated gradually enough that Margaret kept finding reasons to stay. He broke her nose twice. He fractured two of her ribs on a night she remembers with photographic clarity: a Tuesday in November, the smell of shepherd's pie still on the stove, a disagreement about nothing she can now name. She left for the last time in 1978, after he held her head against a kitchen counter until she lost consciousness. She woke alone and drove herself to hospital.

What strikes Margaret, even now, is how thoroughly she compartmentalized. She went to work the following Monday. She sat across from families in crisis and helped them navigate systems of protection and support, and she told no one. She built a career she is genuinely proud of — thirty years specializing in domestic violence services, eventually training other social workers. She understands, intellectually, the dynamics of coercive control better than most people alive. This knowledge has never quite reached the part of her that still flinches when a door slams.

Since retiring twelve years ago, the structure that held everything in place has quietly dissolved. Without the rhythm of cases and colleagues and purpose, the memories have grown louder. She wakes most nights between two and four in the morning with her heart hammering, certain — for a few terrible seconds — that she is back in that kitchen. The dreams are not always dramatic; sometimes she simply dreams that she is waiting for him to come home, and the dread in those dreams is worse than anything involving violence. During the day, she avoids television programmes featuring domestic arguments, avoids certain pieces of music from that era, avoids, she admits with some embarrassment, the entire condiment aisle of her local supermarket because Gerald had a particular brand of brown sauce whose smell once preceded a beating.

She describes a persistent sense of emotional numbness that she has mistaken, for years, for equanimity. She has few close friendships and has not been in a relationship since Gerald. She assumed this was preference. She is beginning to wonder if it is protection. She notices that she feels very little joy, that the things she once loved — gardening, choral singing, her nieces' children — reach her as though through glass.

What troubles Margaret most, and what finally brought her to therapy, is a growing sense of shame she cannot logic her way out of. She spent her professional life telling women that what happened to them was not their fault. She believed it, fiercely and without reservation, for every one of them. She cannot seem to believe it for herself. She sits with that contradiction in the room between sessions, she says, turning it over like a stone she cannot put down. She is eighty years old. She has helped hundreds of people. She is still, in some quiet and persistent way, waiting for a Tuesday evening in November to be over.
